config.title: NSTP 1
config.scope: Midterm: Bill of Rights, Leadership, Health

bank.q: The Bill of Rights is found in which article of the 1987 Philippine Constitution?
bank.why: The slides open with Article III, Bill of Rights.
bank.xq: The 1987 Philippine Constitution sets out the structure of government, the duties of citizens and, in one article, the specific rights that protect every person from abuse of governmental power. In which article of the Constitution is this Bill of Rights found?

bank.term: Concept of a Bill of Rights
bank.q: A declaration and enumeration of a person's rights and privileges which the Constitution is designed to protect against violation by the government, or by individuals or groups of individuals.
bank.why: It is a charter of liberties for the individual and a limitation upon the power of the State.
bank.hint: A declaration and enumeration of rights.
bank.xq: A student explains to her NSTP group that one part of the Constitution lists a person's rights and privileges and is designed to protect them against violation by the government, or by individuals or groups of individuals. Which term best describes the part of the Constitution she is talking about?

bank.term: Bill of Rights as a limitation
bank.q: Aside from being a charter of liberties for the individual, the Bill of Rights is also a...
bank.a: Limitation upon the power of the State
d: Grant of power to the President
List of the duties of citizens
bank.why: It is a charter of liberties for the individual and a limitation upon the power of the State.
bank.xq: The Bill of Rights is commonly described as a charter of liberties that protects the individual. Looking at it from the side of the government instead of the citizen, what else does the Bill of Rights serve as?

bank.q: Section 1: No person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without...
bank.why: Section 1: no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, nor be denied the equal protection of the laws.
bank.xq: Section 1 of Article III guarantees that the State may not simply take away a person's life, freedom or belongings whenever it wishes. According to this section, no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without what?

bank.q: "Nor shall any person be denied the ___ of the laws." (Section 1)
bank.why: Everyone must be treated fairly and equally by the law.
bank.xq: The second half of Section 1 makes sure that the law does not favor some people over others in similar situations. Complete the provision: "...nor shall any person be denied the ___ of the laws."

bank.q: The government cannot take away your life, freedom or belongings unless it follows fair legal procedures. This is the meaning of...
bank.why: Due process: notice of the charges, a fair chance to defend yourself, fair treatment under the law.
bank.xq: A barangay official wants to confiscate a vendor's cart without giving notice, without a hearing and without following any legal procedure. The vendor argues that the government cannot take away a person's life, freedom or belongings unless it follows fair legal procedures. Which constitutional guarantee is the vendor invoking?

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the rights under due process given in the slides?
bank.a: The right to choose your own judge
d: To be given notice of the charges against you
To have a fair chance to defend yourself
To be treated fairly according to the law
bank.why: Due process means notice, a fair chance to defend yourself (e.g. in a trial), and fair treatment according to the law.
bank.xq: Under due process, a person facing a case is entitled to certain protections before the government may act against them. The slides list several of these protections. Which of the following is NOT one of the rights under due process given in the slides?

bank.q: Everyone must be treated fairly and equally by the law regardless of race, religion, gender, social status, nationality or beliefs. This is...
bank.why: Equal protection: the same law applies equally to everyone regardless of background.
bank.xq: A city ordinance gives faster permits to applicants of one religion and makes applicants of other faiths wait longer, even though everything else about their applications is the same. Which guarantee, requiring that everyone be treated fairly and equally by the law regardless of race, religion, gender, social status, nationality or beliefs, is being violated?

bank.q: Section 1 protects a person from being deprived of which three things without due process?
bank.why: No person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law.
bank.xq: Section 1 of the Bill of Rights names three things that the government cannot take from any person unless it first follows due process of law. Which three things does Section 1 protect?

bank.q: The right to exist, to be free from personal restraint or servitude, to contract, to choose one's employment, and to labor make up the...
bank.why: These five together are the right to liberty.
bank.xq: In discussing Section 1, the slides group together the right to exist, to be free from personal restraint or servitude, to contract, to choose one's employment, and to labor. All of these together make up which right?

bank.q: "Every person has the right to live and not be deprived of life or freedom without lawful reason." This explains the...
bank.why: The right to exist is the first part of the right to liberty.
bank.xq: One component of the right to liberty is explained in the slides as: every person has the right to live and not be deprived of life or freedom without lawful reason. Which component of the right to liberty does this explanation refer to?

bank.q: No one can force you into slavery, forced labor or unjust imprisonment. This is the right to be free from...
bank.why: You have the right to move freely and not be imprisoned or enslaved without legal cause.
bank.xq: A factory owner locks workers inside the building and forces them to work without pay, threatening to keep them there until they finish. One part of the right to liberty says no one can force you into slavery, forced labor or unjust imprisonment. The workers' right to be free from what is being violated?

bank.q: Entering into legal agreements such as signing a lease, getting a job or starting a business falls under the right to...
bank.why: The right to contract supports your freedom to make decisions about your personal and economic life.
bank.xq: Maria signs a lease for a boarding house, accepts a part-time job offer, and registers a small online business, all through legal agreements. Entering into legal agreements such as these falls under which part of the right to liberty?

bank.q: "No one can force you to work a certain job against your will." This is the right to...
bank.why: You have the freedom to choose your job or profession.
bank.xq: Paolo's parents insist that he must work in the family's hardware store after graduation, but he wants to work as a nurse. Under the right to liberty, no one can force you to work a certain job against your will. Which right is this?

bank.q: The right to work and earn a living through legal means, with the government protecting safe and fair working conditions, is the right to...
bank.why: The right to labor: work and earn a living; the government must protect safe and fair working conditions.
bank.xq: A construction worker earns a living through legal means, and the government enforces rules that keep the work site safe and the working conditions fair. Which part of the right to liberty covers the right to work and earn a living, with the government protecting safe and fair working conditions?

bank.q: Every person has the legal right to own, use and enjoy what they own, and the law must protect it from being taken, damaged or destroyed. This is the
bank.why: Property includes money, personal belongings, land or houses, and anything you legally own.
bank.xq: Every person may own, use and enjoy what they legally own, and the law must protect it from being taken, damaged or destroyed by others. When a homeowner asks the police to act against someone who is vandalizing her house, she is relying on which right?

bank.q: Under the right to protection of property, "property" includes...
bank.a: Money, personal belongings, land or houses, anything legally owned
d: Only things registered with the government
bank.why: Property includes money, personal belongings, land or houses, and anything you legally own.
bank.xq: A student thinks that the right to protection of property only covers land titles. Her classmate corrects her using the meaning given in the slides. Under the right to protection of property, what does "property" include?

bank.q: Unlawfully killing another person without a qualifying circumstance for murder. This is...
bank.why: Homicide: unlawfully killing another person without a qualifying circumstance for murder. It is a crime against person.
bank.xq: During a heated argument in a basketball court, Leo unlawfully kills another player. Investigators find no treachery, no evident premeditation and no other qualifying circumstance, and the victim is not related to him. Based on the slides, what crime did Leo commit?

bank.q: Unlawfully killing another person with a qualifying circumstance, such as treachery or evident premeditation. This is...
bank.why: Murder: unlawfully killing another person with a qualifying circumstance, such as treachery or evident premeditation. It is a crime against person.
bank.xq: Ramon plans for weeks how to kill his business rival, then waits for him in the dark and attacks him from behind so that the victim has no chance to defend himself. Because the killing involved treachery and evident premeditation, what crime is it?

bank.q: Helping another person take their own life. This is...
bank.why: Giving assistance to suicide: helping another person take their own life. It is a crime against person.
bank.xq: A person does not kill anyone personally, but knowingly provides another person with the means and help to take their own life. According to the list of crimes against persons in the slides, what is this act called?

bank.q: Killing of a newborn baby less than three days old. This is...
bank.why: Infanticide: killing of a newborn baby less than three days old. It is a crime against person.
bank.xq: A mother, overwhelmed after giving birth, kills her own baby when the baby is only two days old. Because the victim is a newborn less than three days old, which crime against persons is this?

bank.q: Unlawfully causing or assisting in the termination of a pregnancy, as defined by law. This is...
bank.why: Abortion: unlawfully causing or assisting in the termination of a pregnancy, as defined by law. It is a crime against person.
bank.xq: A person unlawfully causes, or helps another to bring about, the termination of a pregnancy, in a way defined and punished by law. Among the crimes against persons in the slides, which crime is this?

bank.q: Killing of family members or other close family members. This is...
bank.why: Parricide: killing of family members or other close family members. It is a crime against person.
bank.xq: A man kills his own father during a family dispute. The slides single out the killing of family members or other close family members as a separate crime against persons. What is this crime called?

bank.q: Hurting or injuring another person, such as punching or kicking them. This is...
bank.why: Physical injuries: hurting or injuring another person, such as punching or kicking them. It is a crime against person.
bank.xq: After a minor traffic dispute, one driver punches and kicks the other, hurting him. In the slides, hurting or injuring another person, such as by punching or kicking them, is generally called what?

bank.q: Committing sexual acts against a person under circumstances punishable by law. This is...
bank.why: Rape: committing sexual acts against a person under circumstances punishable by law. It is a crime against person.
bank.xq: The slides list a crime against persons that consists of committing sexual acts against a person under circumstances that are punishable by law, and classify it as an attack on a person's sexual integrity. What crime is this?

bank.q: Causing injuries that result in grave harm, disability, or prolonged incapacity. This is...
bank.why: Serious physical injuries: causing injuries that result in grave harm, disability, or prolonged incapacity. It is a crime against person.
bank.xq: In a fight, a man injures another so badly that the victim becomes disabled and cannot work for months. Because the injuries caused grave harm, disability or prolonged incapacity, what crime is this?

bank.q: Causing minor injuries, such as bruises, that require little or no medical treatment. This is...
bank.why: Slight physical injuries: causing minor injuries, such as bruises, that require little or no medical treatment. It is a crime against person.
bank.xq: During a minor scuffle, a student leaves a classmate with a few bruises that need little or no medical treatment. In the slides' grouping of injuries, causing minor injuries like these is what crime?

bank.q: Taking or carrying away a person against their will. This is...
bank.why: Kidnapping: taking or carrying away a person against their will. It is a crime against liberty.
bank.xq: A group forces a businessman into a van on the street and drives off with him, taking and carrying him away against his will. Among the crimes against liberty in the slides, what is this?

bank.q: Unlawfully preventing someone from leaving a place, e.g. locking a person inside a room without legal authority. This is...
bank.why: Illegal detention: unlawfully preventing someone from leaving a place, e.g. locking a person inside a room without legal authority. It is a crime against liberty.
bank.xq: A landlord who has no legal authority locks a tenant inside a room so that she cannot leave until she pays. Unlawfully preventing someone from leaving a place in this way is which crime against liberty?

bank.q: Unlawfully detaining a person under circumstances specified by law, e.g. abducting someone and holding them captive. This is...
bank.why: Serious illegal detention: unlawfully detaining a person under circumstances specified by law, e.g. abducting someone and holding them captive. It is a crime against liberty.
bank.xq: A person is abducted and held captive for days under circumstances that the law specifically lists as making the detention graver than an ordinary one. Unlawfully detaining a person under these circumstances specified by law is which crime?

bank.q: Forcing someone to do something against their will through violence, threats, or intimidation. This is...
bank.why: Coercion: forcing someone to do something against their will through violence, threats, or intimidation. It is a crime against liberty.
bank.xq: A man forces his neighbor to sign over his tricycle franchise by threatening to hurt the neighbor's family, making him do something against his will through violence, threats or intimidation. What crime against liberty is this?

bank.q: Threatening another person with a serious crime to intimidate or control them. This is...
bank.why: Grave threats: threatening another person with a serious crime to intimidate or control them. It is a crime against liberty.
bank.xq: To make a witness keep quiet, a person tells her that he will burn her house down and harm her children. Threatening another person with a serious crime in order to intimidate or control them is which crime?

bank.q: Arresting or detaining someone without legal grounds or authority, e.g. pretending to be a police officer. This is...
bank.why: Unlawful arrest: arresting or detaining someone without legal grounds or authority, e.g. pretending to be a police officer. It is a crime against liberty.
bank.xq: A civilian puts on a fake police uniform, stops a jeepney driver, and "arrests" him without any legal grounds or authority. Arresting or detaining someone like this falls under which crime against liberty?

bank.q: Recruiting, transporting, or harboring people for exploitation, e.g. a fake job offer. This is...
bank.why: Human trafficking: recruiting, transporting, or harboring people for exploitation, e.g. a fake job offer. It is a crime against liberty.
bank.xq: A recruiter posts an attractive overseas job offer, transports the applicants abroad and then harbors them in a place where they are forced to work for others' profit. Recruiting, transporting or harboring people for exploitation is which crime?

bank.q: A public officer or employee detains someone without legal grounds. This is...
bank.why: Arbitrary detention: a public officer or employee detains someone without legal grounds. It is a crime against liberty.
bank.xq: A municipal employee who holds a public office orders a person kept in the town hall's holding room even though there is no legal ground to detain him. When a public officer or employee detains someone without legal grounds, what crime is committed?

bank.q: Taking another person's property through violence, intimidation, or force. This is...
bank.why: Robbery: taking another person's property through violence, intimidation, or force. It is a crime against property.
bank.xq: A man points a knife at a student in a jeepney and takes her phone and wallet. Because the property was taken through violence, intimidation or force, what crime against property is this?

bank.q: Taking another person's property without permission and without using violence or intimidation. This is...
bank.why: Theft: taking another person's property without permission and without using violence or intimidation. It is a crime against property.
bank.xq: While a store clerk is busy with other customers, a person quietly slips a bottle of shampoo into her bag and leaves without paying, without using any violence or intimidation. What crime against property is this?

bank.q: Theft under circumstances that make it more serious, e.g. an employee entrusted with access steals the employer's money. This is...
bank.why: Qualified theft: theft under circumstances that make it more serious, e.g. an employee entrusted with access steals the employer's money. It is a crime against property.
bank.xq: An accountant who has been entrusted with access to the company's funds secretly takes money belonging to the employer. Because the theft was done under circumstances that make it more serious, what crime is this?

bank.q: Deceiving someone to obtain money or property. This is...
bank.why: Estafa (swindling): deceiving someone to obtain money or property. It is a crime against property.
bank.xq: A person convinces his friends that he can double their money through a fake investment, collects their savings, and disappears. Deceiving someone in order to obtain money or property is which crime against property?

bank.q: Intentionally setting fire to property under circumstances punishable by law. This is...
bank.why: Arson: intentionally setting fire to property under circumstances punishable by law. It is a crime against property.
bank.xq: Angry at his former business partner, a man intentionally sets fire to the partner's warehouse, under circumstances punishable by law. What crime against property is this?

bank.q: Deliberately damaging another person's property without justification, e.g. smashing a neighbor's windows. This is...
bank.why: Malicious mischief: deliberately damaging another person's property without justification, e.g. smashing a neighbor's windows. It is a crime against property.
bank.xq: After a quarrel, a man deliberately smashes his neighbor's windows and slashes the tires of the neighbor's car without any justification. Deliberately damaging another person's property like this is which crime?

bank.q: Taking another person's motor vehicle without consent and with intent to gain. This is...
bank.why: Carnapping: taking another person's motor vehicle without consent and with intent to gain. It is a crime against property.
bank.xq: A person drives off with a car parked outside a mall without the owner's consent, planning to sell it for profit. Taking another person's motor vehicle without consent and with intent to gain is which crime?

bank.q: Buying, receiving, possessing, or dealing in property known to have come from robbery or theft. This is...
bank.why: Fencing: buying, receiving, possessing, or dealing in property known to have come from robbery or theft. It is a crime against property.
bank.xq: A shop owner regularly buys laptops at very low prices from people he knows stole them, and then resells them. Buying, receiving, possessing or dealing in property known to come from robbery or theft is which crime?

bank.q: Unlawfully entering or remaining in certain premises, e.g. entering a fenced lot without permission. This is...
bank.why: Trespass to property: unlawfully entering or remaining in certain premises, e.g. entering a fenced lot without permission. It is a crime against property.
bank.xq: A group of teenagers climbs over the fence of a private resort and stays inside without the owner's permission. Unlawfully entering or remaining in certain premises like this is which crime against property?

bank.q: Falsifying a document or signature under circumstances punishable by law. This is...
bank.why: Forgery: falsifying a document or signature under circumstances punishable by law. It is a crime against property.
bank.xq: A person copies his employer's signature onto a check and alters a document to make it look official, under circumstances punishable by law. Falsifying a document or signature like this is which crime?

bank.q: Parricide is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against persons harm or threaten a person's life, body, or sexual integrity.
bank.xq: The slides group crimes into categories based on what each crime attacks. A man is charged with parricide after killing his own father. Under the slides' grouping, parricide is classified as what type of crime?

bank.q: Infanticide is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against persons harm or threaten a person's life, body, or sexual integrity.
bank.xq: A case of infanticide, the killing of a newborn baby less than three days old, is being discussed in class. Under the categories of crimes used in the slides, how is infanticide classified?

bank.q: Rape is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against persons harm or threaten a person's life, body, or sexual integrity.
bank.xq: The slides group crimes according to whether they harm a person's life, body or sexual integrity, their freedom, or their belongings. Under this grouping, how is rape classified?

bank.q: Kidnapping is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against liberty unlawfully restrict movement, force choices, use threats, or deprive someone of liberty.
bank.xq: A businessman is taken and carried away against his will by armed men. Since the crime mainly attacks the victim's freedom, how do the slides classify kidnapping?

bank.q: Coercion is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against liberty unlawfully restrict movement, force choices, use threats, or deprive someone of liberty.
bank.xq: A person is forced to sign a contract through threats and intimidation, doing something against his will. In the slides' grouping of crimes, how is coercion classified?

bank.q: Human trafficking is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against liberty unlawfully restrict movement, force choices, use threats, or deprive someone of liberty.
bank.xq: Recruiters lure job seekers with fake offers, then transport and harbor them for exploitation. According to the categories in the slides, human trafficking is classified as what type of crime?

bank.q: Grave threats is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against liberty unlawfully restrict movement, force choices, use threats, or deprive someone of liberty.
bank.xq: A person threatens to kill a witness in order to intimidate her and control what she says. In the slides' grouping of crimes, how are grave threats classified?

bank.q: Estafa is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against property illegally take, damage, or destroy someone else's property.
bank.xq: A person deceives his neighbors with a fake investment to obtain their money. Since the crime is aimed at the victims' belongings, how is estafa classified in the slides?

bank.q: Arson is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against property illegally take, damage, or destroy someone else's property.
bank.xq: Someone intentionally sets fire to a rival's store under circumstances punishable by law. In the slides' grouping of crimes, how is arson classified?

bank.q: Fencing is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against property illegally take, damage, or destroy someone else's property.
bank.xq: A buy-and-sell shop knowingly deals in stolen motorcycle parts. Under the categories in the slides, how is fencing classified?

bank.q: Forgery is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against property illegally take, damage, or destroy someone else's property.
bank.xq: An employee falsifies his manager's signature on a document. In the slides' grouping of crimes, how is forgery classified?

bank.q: Carnapping is classified in the slides as a...
bank.why: Crimes against property illegally take, damage, or destroy someone else's property.
bank.xq: A person drives off with a neighbor's car without consent and with intent to gain. In the slides' grouping of crimes, how is carnapping classified?

bank.q: Unlawful acts that harm or threaten a person's life, body, or sexual integrity are called...
bank.why: They are serious violations of human rights and are treated strictly under the law.
bank.xq: Homicide, murder, parricide, infanticide, physical injuries and rape all share one thing: they are unlawful acts that harm or threaten a person's life, body or sexual integrity. What are such acts collectively called?

bank.q: Infanticide is the killing of a newborn baby less than how many days old?
bank.why: Infanticide: killing of a newborn baby less than three days old.
bank.xq: The slides define infanticide by the age of the victim, distinguishing it from other killings such as parricide. Infanticide is the killing of a newborn baby less than how many days old?

bank.q: What makes a killing murder instead of homicide?
bank.a: A qualifying circumstance, such as treachery or evident premeditation
d: The victim is a relative, such as a parent or spouse
The victim is a newborn less than three days old
A deadly weapon, such as a gun or knife, was used
bank.why: Homicide is killing without a qualifying circumstance; murder has one (treachery, evident premeditation).
bank.xq: Two cases both involve one person unlawfully killing another who is not a relative. In the first case it is called homicide, while in the second it is called murder. What makes a killing murder instead of homicide?

bank.q: What separates robbery from theft?
bank.a: Robbery uses violence, intimidation or force
d: Robbery is done by an employee
bank.why: Robbery: through violence, intimidation, or force. Theft: without permission and without violence or intimidation.
bank.xq: In both robbery and theft, a person takes another person's property without permission. A classmate asks what actually makes one robbery and the other theft. What separates robbery from theft?

bank.q: A person knowingly buys stolen cellphones and resells them for profit. This is...
bank.why: Fencing is dealing in property known to come from robbery or theft.
bank.xq: A vendor in a public market knowingly buys stolen cellphones from snatchers at a very low price and resells them to customers for profit. He did not steal the phones himself. What crime did the vendor commit?

bank.q: A person steals someone else's parked motorcycle. This is...
bank.why: Carnapping: taking another person's motor vehicle without consent and with intent to gain.
bank.xq: While the owner is inside a convenience store, a person starts a parked motorcycle without the owner's consent and drives away with it, intending to keep it. Which crime is this?

bank.q: An employee entrusted with access to the workplace steals money belonging to the employer. This is...
bank.why: Theft made more serious by its circumstances (abuse of trust) is qualified theft.
bank.xq: A cashier who was trusted with the keys and access to the store's safe takes money belonging to her employer at the end of her shift. What crime is this?

bank.q: A recruiter deceives a person with a fake job offer and exploits them. This is...
bank.why: Human trafficking: recruiting, transporting, or harboring people for exploitation.
bank.xq: A recruiter offers a young woman a well-paying job abroad that turns out to be fake. Once she arrives, she is held and exploited. Which crime best describes what the recruiter did?

bank.q: A public officer unlawfully holds a person in custody without a legal basis. This is...
bank.why: When the one detaining is a public officer or employee, it is arbitrary detention.
bank.xq: A barangay official, who is a public officer, holds a person in custody in the barangay hall for two days even though there is no legal basis to detain him. What crime did the official commit?

bank.q: A person pretends to be a police officer and arrests someone without authority. This is...
bank.why: Unlawful arrest: arresting or detaining someone without legal grounds or authority.
bank.xq: A private individual who is not a police officer pretends to be one, stops a man on the street, and arrests him without any authority. Which crime is this?

bank.q: A person intentionally smashes a neighbor's windows. This is...
bank.why: Malicious mischief: deliberately damaging another person's property without justification.
bank.xq: Angry about a noise complaint, a man intentionally smashes his neighbor's windows with a baseball bat but does not take anything or enter the house. What crime is this?

bank.q: "The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures..." is Section...
bank.why: Section 2 is the right against unreasonable arrest, search and seizure.
bank.xq: One section of the Bill of Rights begins: "The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures of whatever nature and for any purpose shall be inviolable..." Which section of Article III is this?

bank.q: Under Section 2, a search warrant or warrant of arrest shall issue only upon probable cause determined personally by...
bank.why: Probable cause is determined personally by the judge after examining the complainant and witnesses under oath or affirmation.
bank.xq: Police want a warrant to search a house they suspect is a drug den. Under Section 2, a search warrant or warrant of arrest may only issue upon probable cause determined personally by whom?

bank.q: A search warrant or warrant of arrest shall issue only upon...
bank.why: No warrant shall issue except upon probable cause determined personally by the judge.
bank.xq: Section 2 sets a standard that must be met before any search warrant or warrant of arrest may be issued, so that people are not searched or arrested on mere suspicion. Upon what shall a warrant issue?

bank.q: Before issuing a warrant, the judge examines the complainant and witnesses...
d: In the presence of the accused
bank.why: Probable cause is determined after examination under oath or affirmation of the complainant and the witnesses.
bank.xq: Before issuing a warrant, the judge personally examines the complainant and the witnesses that the complainant produces. According to Section 2, how must the judge examine them?

bank.q: A warrant must particularly describe...
bank.a: The place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized
d: The crime committed and the penalty that may be imposed
The name and rank of the officers who will serve it
The judge's reasons and the evidence of the complainant
bank.why: The warrant must particularly describe the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized.
bank.xq: A warrant that simply says "search the area for illegal items" would be defective. Under Section 2, what must a warrant particularly describe?

bank.q: The protection against unreasonable searches applies to everybody, citizens and aliens in the Philippines, whether accused of a crime or not. This scope is...
bank.why: Scope 1, PERSON: everyone in the Philippines, Filipino or foreign, suspected or not.
bank.xq: The protection against unreasonable searches and seizures covers several things. One of these scopes applies to everybody, citizens and aliens in the Philippines, whether they are accused of a crime or not. Which scope of protection is this?

bank.q: Under the scope of protection, "houses" includes...
bank.a: Garages, warehouses, shops, stores, offices and safety deposit vaults
d: Only the dwelling where a person actually lives and sleeps
Only houses the person owns, not those he rents or borrows
Only buildings with a land title in the person's name
bank.why: HOUSES is not limited to dwelling houses; it covers any private space a person uses or controls.
bank.xq: A store owner claims that Section 2 protects only the house where a person lives, not his shop. Under the scope of protection described in the slides, what does "houses" include?

bank.q: Under the scope of protection, "papers and effects" include...
bank.a: Sealed letters and packages in the mail
bank.why: Papers are private documents; effects are personal belongings; this covers sealed mail too.
bank.xq: Under Section 2, people are protected in their persons, houses, papers and effects. When the slides explain the scope of "papers and effects", which of these do they include?

bank.q: In "papers and effects", "effects" refers to...
bank.why: "Papers" are private documents; "effects" are personal belongings.
bank.xq: In the phrase "papers and effects" in Section 2, "papers" covers documents and letters. What does the word "effects" refer to?

bank.q: A police officer searches a foreign tourist's bag in a mall without any legal basis. Is the tourist protected by Section 2?
bank.a: Yes, the protection covers aliens in the Philippines too
d: No, only Filipino citizens are covered
No, tourists waive their rights at the airport
Only if the tourist has a lawyer
bank.why: The scope PERSON covers citizens and aliens, whether suspected of a crime or not.
bank.xq: A foreign tourist is walking inside a mall in Davao when a police officer stops her and searches her bag, even though there is no warrant, no consent and no other legal basis. Is the tourist protected by Section 2?

bank.q: Police ask James at a bus stop if they can look in his bag, and he says yes. They find drugs. Is the search legal?
d: No, they needed a warrant anyway
No, a bus stop is a public place
Only if a judge was present
bank.why: The slides mark this as a legal search: consent.
bank.xq: Police approach James at a bus stop and politely ask if they may look inside his bag. He freely says yes, and they find illegal drugs inside. James later argues that the search was illegal because there was no warrant. Is the search legal?

bank.q: If James refuses, can the police open and search his bag?
bank.a: No, not without probable cause or a warrant
d: Yes, any bag in public may be searched
bank.why: He may refuse and assert his right against unreasonable searches; they need a warrant or probable cause.
bank.xq: In the same situation, suppose James refuses when the police ask to look inside his bag, and the officers have no warrant and nothing that gives them probable cause. Can the police open and search his bag anyway?

bank.q: An order in writing issued in the name of the People of the Philippines, signed by a judge and directed to a peace officer, commanding him to search for certain personal property and bring it before the court.
bank.why: That is the slides' definition of a search warrant.
bank.xq: It is an order in writing issued in the name of the People of the Philippines, signed by a judge and directed to a peace officer, commanding him to search for certain personal property and bring it before the court. What is this document?

bank.q: A written order issued by the judge to arrest a person or take him into custody to make him answer for an offense.
bank.why: That is the slides' definition of a warrant of arrest.
bank.xq: A judge issues a written order directing officers to arrest a person and take him into custody so that he may answer for an offense. What is this written order called?

bank.q: "The privacy of communication and correspondence shall be inviolable except upon lawful order of the court..." is Section...
bank.why: Section 3 is the right to privacy.
bank.xq: One section of the Bill of Rights says: "The privacy of communication and correspondence shall be inviolable except upon lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law." Which section of Article III is this?

bank.q: Privacy of communication may be set aside upon lawful order of the court, or when...
bank.a: Public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law
d: The person's employer or school asks for it in writing
The media requests it for a story of public interest
A neighbor or relative files a complaint with the barangay
bank.why: Exceptions: a lawful court order, or public safety or order as prescribed by law.
bank.xq: Section 3 protects the privacy of communication and correspondence, but it is not absolute. Apart from a lawful order of the court, when else may this privacy be set aside?

bank.q: Evidence obtained in violation of the right to privacy or against unreasonable searches is...
bank.a: Inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding
bank.why: Section 3(2): such evidence shall be inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding.
bank.xq: Officers secretly read a suspect's private letters without a court order and also search his house without a valid warrant. They want to use what they found against him in court. Under the Bill of Rights, what is the status of this evidence?

bank.q: Anna, a journalist, emails confidential sources. Without a court order, who may open and read her emails?
bank.a: No one: not the police, her employer, or the government
d: Only the police, if they suspect a crime
Only her employer, since it is a work account
bank.why: Her right to privacy of communication is protected; no one may intercept without a valid court order.
bank.xq: Anna is a journalist who exchanges emails with confidential sources. There is no court order and no public safety reason recognized by law. Under Section 3, who may open and read her emails?

bank.q: Anna becomes a suspect in a cybercrime case and a judge grants an order to access her emails. This is...
bank.why: With a lawful court order, authorities may legally access her communications.
bank.xq: Later, Anna becomes a suspect in a cybercrime case, and a judge grants an order allowing investigators to access her emails. How should this access be described under Section 3?

bank.q: The public safety exception to privacy balances the right to privacy with...
bank.a: The government's duty to protect the public
d: The freedom of the press to report the news
The people's right to information on public concern
The right of the accused to bail before conviction
bank.why: It balances your right to privacy and the government's duty to protect the public, used only in rare, serious cases.
bank.xq: Section 3 allows the privacy of communication to be set aside when public safety or order requires it, as prescribed by law. According to the slides, this public safety exception balances the right to privacy with what?

bank.q: Section 4 protects freedom of speech, of expression, of the press, and the right of the people to...
bank.a: Peaceably assemble and petition the government for redress of grievances
d: Travel and change their residence within the limits of law
Form unions, associations or societies for lawful purposes
Access official records and documents on official acts
bank.why: Section 4: no law shall abridge freedom of speech, expression, or the press, or the right to peaceably assemble and petition.
bank.xq: Section 4 provides that no law shall be passed abridging the freedom of speech, of expression, or of the press. Besides these, what other right of the people does Section 4 protect?

bank.q: The right to express thoughts and ideas without government interference, including spoken words, written communication and symbolic actions.
bank.why: Freedom of speech covers spoken words, written communication, and symbolic actions.
bank.xq: A student posts an opinion online, writes a letter to the editor, and wears an armband as a symbol of protest. The right to express thoughts and ideas without government interference, including spoken words, written communication and symbolic actions, is called what?

bank.q: Extends beyond speech to cover art, music and other creative outlets.
bank.why: Freedom of expression protects conveying beliefs through art, music, and other creative outlets.
bank.xq: A group of artists paints a mural, composes a song, and stages a play to share their views. The right that goes beyond spoken words to include any form of expression, such as art, music and other creative outlets, is called what?

bank.q: Ensures that the media can report news and express opinions without censorship or punishment from the government.
bank.why: A free press informs the public and holds power accountable.
bank.xq: A news outlet reports on corruption in a government agency and publishes editorials criticizing officials, without being censored or punished. Which freedom ensures that the media can report news and express opinions this way?

bank.q: Allows individuals to gather peacefully for protests, rallies or meetings.
bank.why: The emphasis on "peaceably" means people gather without violence or disorder.
bank.xq: Students gather in a public plaza for a peaceful rally to call for lower tuition fees. Which right allows individuals to gather peacefully for protests, rallies or meetings?

bank.q: In the right to assemble, the word "peaceably" means people may gather...
d: Only with a permit from the mayor
Only in groups of fewer than ten
bank.why: The emphasis on "peaceably" means they must gather without violence or disorder.
bank.xq: Section 4 protects the right of the people to "peaceably" assemble. A student asks what the word "peaceably" adds to this right. In the right to assemble, "peaceably" means that people may gather how?

bank.q: The ability to make complaints or seek assistance from public officials, including advocating for changes in laws.
bank.why: This is the right to petition the government for redress of grievances.
bank.xq: Residents write a formal complaint to their city council asking for better drainage and lobby their congressman to change a law. The ability to make complaints or seek assistance from the government, including advocating for changes in laws, is which right?

bank.q: Angel, a student, is suspended for a speech criticizing her school's recycling efforts. She believes her suspension violates her right to...
bank.why: The slides use Angel's case to show a person within the scope of protection raising free speech questions.
bank.xq: Angel, a student, gives a speech in class that criticizes her school's recycling efforts. The school suspends her because of the content of her speech. Believing that the suspension is unfair, which right does Angel say was violated?

bank.q: "No law shall be made respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof" is Section...
bank.why: Section 5 is the right to freedom of religion and belief.
bank.xq: One section of the Bill of Rights reads: "No law shall be made respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." Which section of Article III is this?

bank.q: Under Section 5, what shall NOT be required for the exercise of civil or political rights?
bank.why: No religious test shall be required for the exercise of civil or political rights.
bank.xq: A local government requires applicants for a business permit to state and prove their religion before they can vote or run for office in the barangay. Section 5 prohibits this kind of requirement. Under Section 5, what shall NOT be required for the exercise of civil or political rights?

bank.q: The liberty of abode and of changing the same within the limits prescribed by law is part of...
bank.why: Section 6: freedom of movement covers the liberty of abode and the right to travel.
bank.xq: A family decides to move from Davao to Cebu and later to change their address again within the same city. The liberty of abode and of changing the same within the limits prescribed by law is part of which right?

bank.q: The liberty of abode shall not be impaired except upon...
bank.why: Section 6: liberty of abode cannot be impaired except upon lawful order of the court.
bank.xq: Under Section 6, a person is free to choose and change where they live. According to this section, the liberty of abode shall not be impaired except upon what?

bank.q: The right to travel may be impaired only in the interest of...
bank.a: National security, public safety, or public health
bank.why: Section 6: national security, public safety, or public health, as may be provided by law.
bank.xq: Section 6 also protects the right to travel. According to this section, in the interest of which of the following may the right to travel be impaired, as may be provided by law?

bank.q: The right of the people to information on matters of public concern is Section...
bank.why: Section 7 is the right to information.
bank.xq: A student requests copies of the official records and documents behind a new city ordinance. The right of the people to information on matters of public concern is found in which section of Article III?

bank.q: The right to information gives citizens access to official records, documents on official acts, and...
bank.a: Government research data used as a basis for policy development
d: Private emails and messages of public officials
Bank records and deposits of private persons
Sealed letters and parcels sent through the mail
bank.why: Access to official records, documents pertaining to official acts, transactions, or decisions, and government research data used for policy.
bank.xq: Under the right to information, citizens are given access to official records and to documents and papers pertaining to official acts, transactions or decisions. What else does the right to information give citizens access to?

bank.q: The right of the people, in the public and private sectors, to form unions, associations or societies for purposes not contrary to law.
bank.why: Section 8: the right to form unions, associations, or societies shall not be abridged.
bank.xq: Nurses in a private hospital form a union, and government employees form an association, both for purposes not contrary to law. Which right allows people in both the public and private sectors to do this?

bank.q: "Private property shall not be taken for public use without just compensation" is Section...
bank.why: Section 9 is the right to just compensation.
bank.xq: One section of the Bill of Rights states: "Private property shall not be taken for public use without just compensation." Which section of Article III is this?

bank.q: When private property is taken for public use, the owner must receive...
d: A replacement lot of any size
bank.why: Section 9: private property shall not be taken for public use without just compensation.
bank.xq: The government needs a family's lot to widen a highway, which is a public use. Under the Bill of Rights, what must the owner receive when private property is taken for public use?

bank.q: "No law impairing the obligation of contracts shall be passed" is the...
bank.why: Section 10: the government cannot pass a law that unfairly changes or weakens a valid contract.
bank.xq: One provision of the Bill of Rights says "No law impairing the obligation of contracts shall be passed," so that valid agreements made before a law is enacted remain binding. What is this provision called?

bank.q: You sign a valid one-year rental contract. The government then passes a law changing the agreed rent of that existing contract. Which section does this violate?
bank.why: That is the slides' example of the non-impairment clause.
bank.xq: You sign a valid one-year rental contract with your landlord at an agreed monthly rent. A few months later, the government passes a law that changes the rent stated in that existing contract. Which section of the Bill of Rights does this new law violate?

bank.q: Free access to the courts and adequate legal assistance shall not be denied to any person by reason of...
bank.why: Section 11: free access to courts and quasi-judicial bodies shall not be denied by reason of poverty.
bank.xq: A person accused of a crime cannot afford a lawyer and is told that he cannot have his case heard. Section 11 says that free access to the courts and adequate legal assistance shall not be denied to any person by reason of what?

bank.q: The right to remain silent and to have competent and independent counsel belongs to a person under...
bank.why: Section 12: rights of a person under custodial investigation.
bank.xq: Police take a suspect to the station and start questioning him about a robbery. At this point he has the right to remain silent and to have competent and independent counsel, preferably of his own choice. These rights belong to a person under what?

bank.q: If a person under investigation cannot afford counsel...
bank.a: He must be provided with one
d: He must wait until he can afford one
bank.why: Section 12(1): if he cannot afford a lawyer, he must be provided with one.
bank.xq: A suspect under custodial investigation tells the officers that he has no money to hire a lawyer. According to Section 12, what must happen if a person under investigation cannot afford the services of counsel?

bank.q: The rights to remain silent and to counsel cannot be waived except...
bank.a: In writing and in the presence of counsel
bank.why: These rights cannot be waived except in writing and in the presence of counsel.
bank.xq: A suspect under investigation says he wants to give up his right to remain silent and his right to counsel. According to Section 12, these rights cannot be waived except in what way?

bank.q: Which forms of detention are prohibited under Section 12?
d: Detention in a prison after final conviction
Detention for a short time under a valid warrant
Detention in a police station lockup with visits
bank.why: Section 12(2): secret detention places, solitary, incommunicado, or similar forms of detention are prohibited.
bank.xq: Section 12 lists places and forms of detention that are prohibited because they hide the detainee from family and lawyers. Which forms of detention are prohibited under Section 12?

bank.q: A confession obtained through threats or torture is...
d: Admissible if the accused signs it
bank.why: Section 12(3): it cannot be used as evidence against the suspect.
bank.xq: During questioning, officers threaten a suspect and torture him until he signs a confession admitting to the crime. Under Section 12, what is the status of a confession obtained in this way?

bank.q: Under Section 12(4), a police officer who tortures a suspect may face...
bank.a: Criminal and civil penalties, plus compensation for the victim
d: Only a written warning in his service record
Transfer to another station, with no charges filed
No penalty at all, if the suspect is later found guilty
bank.why: The law provides penal and civil sanctions, plus compensation and rehabilitation for victims and their families.
bank.xq: A police officer tortures a suspect during custodial investigation to force him to talk. Under Section 12(4), what may the officer face, and what may the victim receive?

bank.q: The right to bail and against excessive bail is Section...
bank.why: Section 13: right to bail and against excessive bail.
bank.xq: One section of the Bill of Rights says all persons, except those charged with offenses punishable by reclusion perpetua when evidence of guilt is strong, shall be bailable before conviction, and that excessive bail shall not be required. Which section is this?

bank.q: Who may NOT be granted bail?
bank.a: Those charged with reclusion perpetua offenses when evidence of guilt is strong
d: Anyone charged with a crime, until the trial is over
Those who cannot pay the full bail amount set by the court
First-time offenders charged with minor crimes like theft
bank.why: All persons are bailable before conviction except those charged with reclusion perpetua offenses when evidence of guilt is strong.
bank.xq: Section 13 says that all persons shall be bailable before conviction, with one exception. Based on Section 13, who may NOT be granted bail?

bank.q: Reclusion perpetua is a very serious punishment, like...
bank.why: Reclusion perpetua is like life imprisonment (e.g. for murder, drug trafficking).
bank.xq: Section 13 denies bail to those charged with offenses punishable by reclusion perpetua when evidence of guilt is strong. In the slides, reclusion perpetua is explained as a very serious punishment, similar to what?

bank.q: Bail paid with money or property is called...
bank.why: Bail can be paid with money or property (surety), or be a release on recognizance.
bank.xq: An accused is allowed temporary release before trial after his family puts up money as a guarantee that he will return to court. Bail that is paid with money or property is called what?

bank.q: Release without paying, based on a promise to return for trial, especially for poor or low-risk individuals, is...
bank.why: Recognizance: release on a promise to return for trial.
bank.xq: A poor, low-risk accused is released without paying any amount, based only on his promise to return for trial. What is this type of release called?

bank.q: Is the right to bail impaired when the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus is suspended?
bank.why: The right to bail shall not be impaired even when the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus is suspended.
bank.xq: During a rebellion, the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus is suspended. An accused who is otherwise entitled to bail asks if he can still post bail. According to Section 13, is the right to bail impaired when the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus is suspended?

bank.q: The right to bail protects which principle?
bank.why: Bail before conviction protects the presumption that everyone is innocent until proven guilty.
bank.xq: Because an accused has not yet been convicted, the law allows him temporary liberty while his case is being tried instead of keeping him in jail. Which principle does the right to bail protect?

bank.q: Section 14 covers the...
d: Rights of a person under custodial investigation
bank.why: Section 14: rights of the accused, to ensure a fair trial.
bank.xq: One section of the Bill of Rights says no person shall be held to answer for a criminal offense without due process, and that the accused is presumed innocent and entitled to be heard, to a speedy, impartial and public trial, and to meet witnesses face to face. What does Section 14 cover?

bank.q: In all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall be presumed...
bank.a: Innocent until the contrary is proved
d: Innocent only if he has a lawyer
bank.why: Section 14(2): presumed innocent until the contrary is proved.
bank.xq: In a criminal case, the prosecution must prove the charges against the accused, who does not have to prove that he did nothing wrong. Under Section 14, in all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall be presumed what?

bank.q: After arraignment, trial may proceed even without the accused, provided that...
bank.a: He was duly notified and his failure to appear is unjustifiable
d: The judge and the prosecutor both agree to it
The accused is a foreigner who has left the country
The crime is minor and the penalty is only a fine
bank.why: Section 14(2): trial in absentia after arraignment if he was duly notified and his absence is unjustifiable.
bank.xq: After arraignment, an accused stops attending his trial. Under Section 14, the trial may proceed even without the accused, provided that what condition is met?

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the rights of the accused listed in the slides?
bank.why: Listed: presumed innocent, remain silent, a lawyer, fair and speedy trial, know the charges, confront witnesses.
bank.xq: Section 14 lists several rights of the accused, such as the right to be heard by himself and counsel and to have a speedy, impartial and public trial. Which of the following is NOT one of the rights of the accused listed in the slides?

bank.q: The right of the accused to question the people testifying against them is the right to...
bank.why: The accused can meet the witnesses face to face and question them.
bank.xq: During trial, the defense lawyer is allowed to face and question each witness that the prosecution presents. The right of the accused to question witnesses presented against them is the right to what?

bank.q: The right to have compulsory process secures...
bank.a: The attendance of witnesses and production of evidence in the accused's behalf
d: A lawyer for free, chosen by the court if he has none
His release on bail while the trial is going on
A trial held in his hometown, near his family
bank.why: Section 14(2): compulsory process to secure attendance of witnesses and production of evidence in his behalf.
bank.xq: An accused needs a key witness to testify and certain records to be produced, but the witness refuses to come voluntarily. Under Section 14, the right to have compulsory process secures what?

bank.q: A court order requiring authorities to bring a detained person before the court and explain the legal reason for the detention.
bank.why: Section 15: it protects people from unlawful detention.
bank.xq: A man is detained, and his lawyer asks the court for an order requiring the authorities to bring him before the court and explain the legal reason for his detention. What is this court order called?

bank.q: The privilege of the writ of habeas corpus may be suspended only in cases of...
bank.a: Invasion or rebellion, when public safety requires it
d: An economic crisis that threatens the nation
Election period, to keep peace at the polls
bank.why: Section 15: only in invasion or rebellion when public safety requires it.
bank.xq: The privilege of the writ of habeas corpus protects people from illegal detention, but Section 15 allows it to be suspended in certain situations. In which cases may the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus be suspended?

bank.q: Mr. Ramos is arrested without clear charges and held for several days. What can his family file?
bank.a: A petition for a writ of habeas corpus
bank.why: The court then orders the police to present him before a judge; if the detention is unlawful, he is released.
bank.xq: Mr. Ramos is arrested without being told of any clear charges and is held for several days. His family wants a court to order the authorities to bring him before it and explain why he is being detained. What can his family file?

bank.q: All persons shall have the right to a speedy disposition of their cases before all judicial, quasi-judicial, or administrative bodies. This is Section...
bank.why: Section 16: right to a speedy disposition of cases.
bank.xq: A case has been pending in an administrative office for years without any decision. One section of the Bill of Rights says all persons shall have the right to a speedy disposition of their cases before all judicial, quasi-judicial or administrative bodies. Which section is this?

bank.q: "No person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself" is the right against...
bank.why: Section 17: the right against self-incrimination.
bank.xq: During trial, the prosecutor tries to force the accused to take the witness stand and testify against himself. Section 17 says "No person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself." This is the right against what?

bank.q: The right against self-incrimination upholds the idea that the burden of proof lies with...
bank.why: The burden of proof lies with the government, not the individual.
bank.xq: Because no person can be compelled to be a witness against himself, the accused does not have to help prove his own guilt. The right against self-incrimination upholds the idea that the burden of proof lies with whom?

bank.q: "No person shall be detained solely by reason of his political beliefs and aspirations" is Section...
bank.why: Section 18: the right to political beliefs and aspirations.
bank.xq: An activist is arrested and kept in jail only because of his political beliefs and aspirations, even though he has committed no crime. One section of the Bill of Rights says no person shall be detained solely by reason of his political beliefs and aspirations. Which section is this?

bank.q: Involuntary servitude in any form shall not exist except...
bank.a: As a punishment for a crime of which the party has been duly convicted
d: When a person fails to pay a debt he owes
During a state of calamity declared by the President
When an employer orders it as part of the contract
bank.why: Section 18(2): no involuntary servitude except as punishment for a crime after conviction.
bank.xq: Section 18 states that involuntary servitude in any form shall not exist, with only one exception. According to Section 18, when may involuntary servitude exist?

bank.q: Excessive fines, and cruel, degrading or inhuman punishment are prohibited by Section...
bank.why: Section 19: prohibition against cruel, degrading or inhuman punishment.
bank.xq: One section of the Bill of Rights says excessive fines shall not be imposed, and that cruel, degrading or inhuman punishment shall not be inflicted. Which section of Article III is this?

bank.q: Under Section 19, the death penalty shall not be imposed unless...
bank.a: For compelling reasons involving heinous crimes, Congress provides for it
d: The President orders it for crimes against the state
The victim's family requests it in a written petition
The accused pleads guilty and waives his right to appeal
bank.why: Neither shall the death penalty be imposed unless, for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes, Congress provides for it.
bank.xq: Section 19 limits when the death penalty may be imposed. According to this section, the death penalty shall not be imposed unless what condition is met?

bank.q: Under Section 19, any death penalty already imposed shall be reduced to...
bank.why: Any death penalty already imposed shall be reduced to reclusion perpetua.
bank.xq: Section 19 also deals with death penalties that had already been imposed when the Constitution took effect. Under Section 19, any death penalty already imposed shall be reduced to what?

bank.q: Under Section 19, fines must be...
d: As high as possible to deter crime
bank.why: The government cannot charge unfairly large fines; fines must be proportionate.
bank.xq: A court imposes a very large fine for a minor traffic violation in order to scare others. Section 19 prohibits excessive fines. Under Section 19, how must fines be set?

bank.q: Mental abuse, threats, isolation and humiliation of prisoners are examples of which prohibited punishment?
bank.why: Physical: beating, torture. Psychological: mental abuse, threats, isolation, humiliation. Degrading: disrespects human dignity.
bank.xq: In a detention facility, guards repeatedly threaten prisoners, keep them isolated and humiliate them in front of others, but do not physically hurt them. Mental abuse, threats, isolation and humiliation of prisoners are examples of which prohibited punishment?

bank.q: Under Section 19, a detainee is someone who is...
bank.why: Prisoners are already convicted; detainees are still awaiting trial or investigation. Both are protected.
bank.xq: Section 19 also protects detainees from being kept in sub-standard or inadequate penal facilities. As used in Section 19, a detainee is someone who is in what situation?

bank.q: "No person shall be imprisoned for debt or non-payment of a poll tax" is Section...
bank.why: Section 20: non-imprisonment for debts.
bank.xq: A man who fails to pay his credit card bill is threatened with jail by the collection agency. One section of the Bill of Rights says "No person shall be imprisoned for debt or non-payment of a poll tax." Which section is this?

bank.q: Section 20 says no person shall be imprisoned for debt or for non-payment of...
bank.why: No person shall be imprisoned for debt or non-payment of a poll tax.
bank.xq: Section 20 protects people from going to jail simply because they owe money. According to this section, no person shall be imprisoned for debt or for the non-payment of what?

bank.q: "No person shall be twice put in jeopardy of punishment for the same offense" is the...
bank.why: Section 21: double jeopardy.
bank.xq: A person who was already acquitted of a crime is charged again for the very same offense. The Bill of Rights says "No person shall be twice put in jeopardy of punishment for the same offense." What is this provision called?

bank.q: If an act is punished by both a law and an ordinance, conviction or acquittal under either...
bank.a: Bars another prosecution for the same act
d: Allows a second trial under the other
bank.why: Section 21: conviction or acquittal under either shall constitute a bar to another prosecution for the same act.
bank.xq: A single act is punished both by a national law and by a city ordinance, and the person is tried and acquitted under the ordinance. Under Section 21, what is the effect of a conviction or acquittal under either the law or the ordinance?

bank.q: A person is found not guilty of theft by a court with proper jurisdiction. Can they be tried again for the same offense?
bank.a: Generally no, because of double jeopardy
d: Yes, if new evidence appears the next day
bank.why: A person cannot be tried or punished twice for the same offense after a valid acquittal or conviction.
bank.xq: A person is charged with theft, tried by a court with proper jurisdiction, and found not guilty. A week later the prosecutor wants to try the same person again for the same theft. Can the person be tried again for the same offense?

bank.q: "No ex post facto law or bill of attainder shall be enacted" is Section...
bank.why: Section 22 is the last section discussed in the slides.
bank.xq: One section of the Bill of Rights prevents Congress from passing laws that punish acts retroactively or that punish people without a trial: "No ex post facto law or bill of attainder shall be enacted." Which section is this?

bank.q: A law that punishes an act that was not a crime when it was committed, or makes the punishment harsher retroactively.
bank.why: An ex post facto law retroactively changes the legal consequences of past actions.
bank.xq: A new law punishes an act that was not a crime at the time it was committed, or makes the punishment for a past act harsher after the fact. Which type of law is this, prohibited by Section 22?

bank.q: A law that declares a specific person or group guilty and punishes them without a judicial trial.
bank.why: A bill of attainder punishes without a judicial trial.
bank.xq: Congress passes a measure that names a specific person or group, declares them guilty, and punishes them without any judicial trial. What is this kind of law called?

bank.q: A person legally parks today. Tomorrow a new law makes that past parking a crime and punishes them. This is...
bank.why: The new law punishes an act that was legal when it was done.
bank.xq: Today, a person parks legally on a street where parking is allowed. Tomorrow, a new law makes parking there a crime and punishes everyone who parked there before the law was passed, including this person. What kind of law is this?

bank.q: Congress passes a law declaring a named person guilty of a crime and ordering their imprisonment without a court trial. This is...
bank.why: Declaring guilt and punishing without a judicial trial is a bill of attainder.
bank.xq: Congress passes a law that names a particular person, declares that he is guilty of a crime, and orders his imprisonment without any court trial. Which type of law, prohibited by Section 22, is this?

bank.q: Article III, Section 1 is the...
d: Right against unreasonable searches and seizures
Freedom of speech, expression, press, assembly and petition
bank.why: Section 1: Due process and equal protection. No one is deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process.
bank.xq: The first section of Article III says no person shall be deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law, nor be denied the equal protection of the laws. What is Article III, Section 1 known as?

bank.term: Due process and equal protection: section number

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the 7 habits of highly effective people?

bank.q: The process of working collaboratively with a group of people in order to achieve a goal.
bank.why: Teamwork: working collaboratively with a group of people to achieve a goal.

bank.q: The art of arranging, organizing, scheduling and budgeting one's time.

bank.a: Generating more effective work and productivity

Influencing and guiding followers toward goals
Working collaboratively with a group of people

d: Decide quickly and alone so the group saves time
Reward followers only when expectations are met
Avoid every risk and uncertainty the group faces

bank.q: The summary slide says a good leader is adept in...
bank.why: From the last slide.

bank.q: The process that involves selecting the most logical choice from among two or more options.
bank.why: Decision-making: selecting the most logical choice from two or more options.

bank.q: Which is the first consideration in decision-making?
bank.why: Identify alternatives → evaluate options against the objectives → select the best after in-depth evaluation.

bank.q: In decision-making, determining which option meets the decision objectives is the...
bank.why: Second consideration: evaluation.

bank.q: Choosing the best option after an in-depth evaluation is the...
bank.why: Third consideration: selection.

bank.q: "Compromising various possibilities after all opinions have been heard." Which kind of involvement in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Consensus or agreement: Compromising various possibilities after all opinions have been heard.

bank.q: "Voting is considered the most effective way to make a decision." Which kind of involvement in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Majority: Voting is considered the most effective way to make a decision.

bank.q: "Not consciously organized; a few powerful personalities dominate the group, often unconsciously." Which kind of involvement in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Minority: Not consciously organized; a few powerful personalities dominate the group, often unconsciously.

bank.q: "Agreement is reached without much verbal discussion; leads to unanimous decisions but is rarely applied to important issues." Which kind of involvement in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Silent consensus: Agreement is reached without much verbal discussion; leads to unanimous decisions but is rarely applied to important issues.

bank.q: "A small group whose members plan beforehand to get their way in decision-making." Which kind of involvement in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Clique: A small group whose members plan beforehand to get their way in decision-making.

bank.q: "One person makes a suggestion and another commends it." Which kind of involvement in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Handclasp: One person makes a suggestion and another commends it.

bank.q: "Quickly made, but the decider may have trouble later getting voluntary support to implement it." Which kind of involvement in decision-making is this?
bank.why: One-person decision: Quickly made, but the decider may have trouble later getting voluntary support to implement it.

bank.q: "The group makes a decision by not making a decision at all." Which kind of involvement in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Plop: The group makes a decision by not making a decision at all.

bank.q: The officers decide by a show of hands, and the option with more votes wins. Which kind of decision-making is this?
bank.why: Majority: voting is considered the most effective way to make a decision.

bank.q: Three officers meet secretly before the meeting to make sure their proposal is the one chosen. Which kind of decision-making is this?
bank.why: Clique: a small group whose members plan beforehand to get their way in decision-making.

bank.q: No one responds to a suggestion, so the issue is dropped and nothing is ever decided. Which kind of decision-making is this?
bank.why: Plop: the group makes a decision by not making a decision at all.

bank.q: The president decides alone in minutes, but later the members are unwilling to help carry it out. Which kind of decision-making is this?
bank.why: One-person decision: quickly made, but the decider may have trouble later getting voluntary support to implement it.

bank.q: One member suggests a venue, another says "Great idea!", and it is adopted. Which kind of decision-making is this?
bank.why: Handclasp: one person makes a suggestion and another commends it.

bank.q: After everyone gives an opinion, the group compromises on a plan everyone can accept. Which kind of decision-making is this?
bank.why: Consensus or agreement: compromising various possibilities after all opinions have been heard.

bank.q: Everyone nods and agrees right away without much discussion. Which kind of decision-making is this?
bank.why: Silent consensus: agreement is reached without much verbal discussion; leads to unanimous decisions but is rarely applied to important issues.

bank.q: Two loud, influential members end up steering the decision while the others just go along. Which kind of decision-making is this?
bank.why: Minority: not consciously organized; a few powerful personalities dominate the group, often unconsciously.

bank.q: How many kinds of involvement in decision-making are listed in the slides?
bank.why: Consensus, majority, minority, silent consensus, clique, handclasp, one-person decision, plop.

bank.q: "Brings division and disagreement." Which difficulty in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Fear of consequences: Brings division and disagreement.

bank.q: "A person who belongs to different groups ends up divided about decisions." Which difficulty in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Conflicting loyalties: A person who belongs to different groups ends up divided about decisions.

bank.q: "Personal differences evoke feelings among members that interfere with sound decision-making." Which difficulty in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Interpersonal conflicts: Personal differences evoke feelings among members that interfere with sound decision-making.

bank.q: "A secret motive, for reasons a member does not share with the group, hinders decision-making." Which difficulty in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Hidden agenda: A secret motive, for reasons a member does not share with the group, hinders decision-making.

bank.q: "Using rigid procedures, substituting personal opinions for adequate information, and disregarding consultation." Which difficulty in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Blundering methods: Using rigid procedures, substituting personal opinions for adequate information, and disregarding consultation.

bank.q: "The leader restricts the expression of opinions and fails to help select appropriate methods." Which difficulty in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Inadequate leadership: The leader restricts the expression of opinions and fails to help select appropriate methods.

bank.q: "Different groups or individuals within an organization have opposing interests." Which difficulty in decision-making is this?
bank.why: Clash of interest: Different groups or individuals within an organization have opposing interests.

bank.q: A member votes against a fundraising booth because it would compete with his own business, but he never tells the group why. This is...
bank.why: A secret motive not shared with the group.

bank.q: A student belongs to both the dance troupe and the student council, which want different dates for an event, and cannot decide which to support. This is...
bank.why: Being a member of different groups leads to divided loyalties.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the difficulties in decision-making in the slides?
bank.why: The 7: fear of consequences, conflicting loyalties, interpersonal conflicts, hidden agenda, blundering methods, inadequate leadership, clash of interest.

bank.q: A conceptual model that shows the interactions between the environment, the host and an infectious (or abiotic) agent.
bank.why: The disease triangle (epidemiologic triad): host, agent, environment.

bank.q: What are the three parts of the disease triangle?
bank.why: Host, agent and environment.

bank.q: The disease triangle can be used to predict epidemiological outcomes in...
bank.why: In plant health and public health, in local and global communities.

bank.q: In the disease triangle, which part includes: Age, sex, race, genetic profile, previous diseases, immune status, religion, customs, occupation, marital status, family background?
bank.why: Host: Age, sex, race, genetic profile, previous diseases, immune status, religion, customs, occupation, marital status, family background.

bank.q: In the disease triangle, which part includes: Temperature, humidity, altitude, crowding, housing, neighborhood, water, milk, food, pollution, noise?
bank.why: Environment: Temperature, humidity, altitude, crowding, housing, neighborhood, water, milk, food, pollution, noise.

bank.q: In the disease triangle, which part includes: Biologic, chemical, physical and nutritional factors?
bank.why: Agent: Biologic, chemical, physical and nutritional factors.

bank.q: In the disease triangle, "Bacteria and viruses" are which kind of agent?
bank.why: Biologic agents: bacteria and viruses.

bank.q: In the disease triangle, "Poison, alcohol and smoke" are which kind of agent?
bank.why: Chemical agents: poison, alcohol and smoke.

bank.q: In the disease triangle, "Trauma, radiation and fire" are which kind of agent?
bank.why: Physical agents: trauma, radiation and fire.

bank.q: In the disease triangle, "Lack or excess" are which kind of agent?
bank.why: Nutritional agents: lack or excess.

bank.q: Diseases that are spread from one person to another, are "catching", and are caused by germs or pathogens.
bank.why: Communicable: spread person to person, caused by germs or pathogens.

bank.q: According to the slides, examples of pathogens include...
bank.a: Viruses, bacteria, parasitic worms and fungi
bank.why: Pathogens: viruses, bacteria, parasitic worms and fungi.

bank.q: According to the slides' table, what is the mode of spread of cholera?
