bank.q: According to the slides' table, what is the mode of spread of typhoid?
d: Bite wound exposed to dust or a rusted item
bank.why: Typhoid: contaminated food and water.

bank.q: According to the slides' table, what is the mode of spread of hepatitis (jaundice)?
d: Bite wound exposed to dust or a rusted item

bank.q: According to the slides' table, what is the mode of spread of influenza (flu)?
d: Bite wound exposed to dust or a rusted item

bank.q: According to the slides' table, what is the mode of spread of tuberculosis (TB)?
d: Bite wound exposed to dust or a rusted item

d: Bite wound exposed to dust or a rusted item

bank.why: Tetanus: bite wound exposed to dust or a rusted item.

bank.q: A febrile disease caused by one of four closely related virus serotypes of the genus Flavivirus, family Flaviviridae.

bank.q: Dengue is caused by one of how many closely related virus serotypes?
bank.why: Four closely related serotypes.

bank.q: The dengue virus belongs to which genus?
bank.why: Genus Flavivirus, family Flaviviridae.

bank.q: The dengue virus belongs to which family?
bank.why: Family Flaviviridae.

bank.q: Which of these is among the dengue fever symptoms shown in the slides?

bank.q: Rash, rapid pulse, redness of the eye, redness of the throat and pain in the bones are symptoms of...
bank.why: From the dengue fever symptoms infographic.

bank.q: According to the mosquito-bite prevention slide, mosquitoes that spread dengue, chikungunya and Zika are...

Biters only at dawn and dusk, never at noon
Harmless in the daytime, active only indoors

bank.why: Wear long sleeves and long pants, use repellent, and treat clothing with permethrin.

Store water in open drums beside the house

bank.why: Malaria: a parasite carried by a mosquito.

bank.q: Which malaria parasite is the most serious?

bank.q: Malaria is spread by which vector?
bank.why: The female Anopheles mosquito.

bank.q: Malaria symptoms begin...

d: Less than one day to five days after infection

White coating on the tongue, enlarged liver and spleen
Loss of skin elasticity, low blood pressure, increased thirst

bank.q: Malaria treatment with prescription drugs depends on...

The season and the weather in the area
The number of mosquito bites on the body

bank.q: How is malaria prevented according to the slides?
bank.a: Anti-malarial drugs and avoiding being bitten
d: Boiling drinking water and washing hands
Avoiding poultry, birds and their droppings
bank.why: Prevention: anti-malarial drugs, avoid being bitten.

bank.q: An acute intestinal infection caused by ingestion of food or water contaminated with a bacterium, with a short incubation period.
bank.why: Cholera: Vibrio cholerae in food or water.

bank.q: Cholera is caused by which bacterium?
bank.why: Vibrio cholerae (the slide writes "Vibrio cholera").

bank.q: The incubation period of cholera lasts...
bank.a: Less than one day to five days
d: A week up to a year
bank.why: A short incubation period: less than one day to five days.

bank.q: Loss of skin elasticity, low blood pressure, increased thirst, rapid weight loss, vomiting and diarrhea are signs of...
bank.why: From the cholera infographic.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the cholera prevention measures in the slides?
d: Drink water that is boiled or chlorinated
Wash fruits and vegetables with safe water
Cook food properly and eat only hot food

bank.q: According to the cholera poster, you should report immediately to the nearest health facility if you have...

bank.q: An infection caused by influenza A viruses found chiefly in birds, but infections can occur in humans.
bank.why: Avian influenza: influenza A viruses chiefly in birds.

bank.q: Avian influenza (bird flu) is caused by which type of influenza virus?
bank.why: Avian influenza A viruses.

bank.q: Which is among the avian flu symptoms in the slides?
bank.why: Avian flu: cough, high fever, fatigue, headache, nose bleed, runny nose, upset stomach, loss of appetite.

bank.q: To prevent avian influenza, the slides say we should...
bank.a: Avoid touching poultry, birds and their droppings
d: Use insect repellent and wear long sleeves
Reduce salt intake and exercise regularly
bank.why: Also cook poultry and eggs thoroughly and wash hands with liquid soap and water.

bank.q: When going abroad, the bird flu prevention slide says to avoid visiting...
bank.a: Wet markets, live poultry markets and farms in affected areas
d: Hospitals, clinics and drugstores in the area
Malls, cinemas and crowded bus terminals
bank.why: If you feel unwell after the trip, wear a surgical mask, seek medical advice and reveal your travel details.

bank.q: A flu virus also known as the swine flu.
bank.why: H1N1 = swine flu.

bank.a: Two genes from flu viruses among pigs and two from flu viruses among birds
d: Four genes from flu viruses which circulate among pigs
Two genes from flu viruses among pigs and two from flu viruses among humans
Two genes from flu viruses among birds and two from flu viruses among humans

bank.why: Systemic: fever.

bank.q: In the H1N1 symptom diagram, "lethargy and lack of appetite" are listed under which group?
bank.why: Psychological: lethargy and lack of appetite.

bank.q: In the H1N1 symptom diagram, "runny nose and sore throat" are listed under which group?
bank.why: Nasopharynx: runny nose and sore throat.

bank.q: In the H1N1 symptom diagram, "coughing" are listed under which group?
bank.why: Respiratory: coughing.

bank.q: In the H1N1 symptom diagram, "nausea and vomiting" are listed under which group?

bank.q: In the H1N1 symptom diagram, "diarrhea" are listed under which group?
bank.why: Intestinal: diarrhea.

bank.q: According to the flu prevention tips, influenza is the only respiratory virus that is preventable by...
bank.why: "Get vaccinated: influenza is the only respiratory virus preventable by vaccination."

bank.q: The H1N1 prevention tips say to stay home for how long after your fever goes away?
bank.why: Stay home for a full 24 hours after your fever goes away.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the H1N1 prevention tips in the slides?

bank.q: Why do the flu prevention tips say not to touch your face?

d: It spreads the virus to the people around you
It causes rashes and sores on the skin of the face
It weakens the CD4 (T-helper) cells of the immune system
bank.why: From the H1N1 prevention infographic.

bank.q: An acute illness most often caused by Salmonella typhi bacteria.
bank.why: Typhoid: Salmonella typhi; Salmonella paratyphi usually causes a less severe infection.

bank.q: Which related bacterium usually leads to a less severe typhoid infection?

bank.q: How is typhoid spread according to the slides?
bank.a: A human carrier deposits the bacteria in water or food, which then spreads to others
d: Through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito
Through droplets from infected birds and their droppings
Through a bite wound exposed to dust or a rusted item

bank.q: White coating on the tongue, enlarged liver and spleen, rash on the body and ulcers in the intestine are signs of...
bank.why: From the typhoid fever diagram.

bank.q: Which is among the symptoms of typhoid in the slides?
bank.why: Typhoid: malaise, loss of appetite, hallucinations/delirium, abdominal pain, ulcers, diarrhea, constipation, severe headache, high fever, encephalitis, dehydration, skin rashes.

bank.q: In typhoid prevention, eggs should be...
bank.a: Thoroughly cooked and never eaten raw
bank.why: Also avoid preserving food at warm temperature and reheating food.

bank.q: Which protective health measure for typhoid is in the slides?
bank.a: Clean water, adequate sewage disposal and control of flies
d: Insect repellent, window screens and mosquito nets
Avoiding poultry, wet markets and bird droppings
Reducing salt intake and regular physical activity

bank.q: A virus that attacks the body's immune system, specifically the CD4 (T-helper) cells, which help fight infections.
bank.why: HIV: Human Immunodeficiency Virus.

bank.q: HIV stands for...
bank.why: HIV = Human Immunodeficiency Virus, the virus that attacks the body's immune system.

bank.q: AIDS stands for...
bank.why: AIDS = Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome, the most advanced stage of HIV infection, when the immune system is badly damaged.

bank.q: The most advanced stage of HIV infection, when the immune system is severely damaged and the person is vulnerable to opportunistic infections and certain cancers.
bank.why: AIDS: the most advanced stage of HIV infection.

bank.q: HIV specifically attacks which cells?
bank.why: CD4 (T-helper) cells help fight infections.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the ways HIV is transmitted in the slides?
bank.a: Sharing a meal with an infected person
d: Mother-to-child during pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding
bank.why: HIV spreads through specific body fluids: sex, needles, transfusions, mother-to-child, occupational exposure.

bank.q: Why is HIV transmission through blood transfusions rare today?
d: Because HIV cannot survive in blood
Because transfusions are no longer done
bank.why: Blood transfusions with infected blood are rare today due to screening.

bank.q: A nurse is pricked by a used needle while working in the hospital. This route of HIV transmission is called...
bank.why: Occupational exposure, such as needlestick injuries in healthcare settings.

bank.q: The early stage (acute HIV infection) appears how long after exposure?
bank.why: Early stage: 2–4 weeks after exposure, flu-like symptoms that may go unnoticed.

bank.q: Fever, fatigue, swollen lymph nodes, sore throat, rash and muscle and joint pain that resemble the flu belong to which stage?
bank.why: The early stage's symptoms resemble the flu and may go unnoticed.

bank.q: Often no symptoms for several years; the virus remains active but reproduces at low levels. Which stage is this?
bank.why: Clinical latency: chronic HIV infection.

bank.q: Without treatment, the clinical latency stage can last...
bank.why: Without treatment: 5–10 years.

bank.q: Rapid weight loss, persistent fever or night sweats, chronic diarrhea and recurrent infections such as tuberculosis and pneumonia happen in which stage?
bank.why: The AIDS stage: the immune system is severely damaged.

bank.q: Stigma, discrimination, stress or depression among people living with HIV are which effect of HIV/AIDS?
bank.why: The four effects: immune system failure, neurological problems, social and psychological impacts, economic effects.

bank.q: Memory problems, difficulty thinking or nerve damage are which effect of HIV/AIDS?
bank.why: HIV can affect the brain and nerves.

bank.q: The cost of medical care and difficulty working due to illness are which effect of HIV/AIDS?
bank.why: They may affect income and finances.

bank.q: Is there a cure for HIV?
bank.a: No, but it can be controlled with proper treatment
d: Yes, a full course of antibiotics cures it
Yes, a vaccine given after exposure cures it
No, and treatment cannot slow it down at all
bank.why: No cure; ART controls it, and people with HIV can live long, healthy lives.

bank.q: What is the main treatment for HIV?
bank.why: ART: a combination of medicines.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the goals of antiretroviral therapy in the slides?
bank.a: Completely remove the virus from the body
bank.why: ART suppresses the virus, restores and protects the immune system, prevents progression to AIDS and reduces transmission risk.

bank.q: Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is for...
bank.a: People at high risk of HIV
d: People already in the AIDS stage
bank.why: PrEP: for people at high risk; PEP: emergency treatment after exposure.

bank.q: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is emergency treatment given within how long after a potential exposure?
bank.why: PEP: within 72 hours.

bank.q: To prevent mother-to-child transmission, pregnant women with HIV should...
bank.why: Pregnant women with HIV should take ART.

bank.q: Which is one of the HIV prevention measures in the slides?
d: Use insect repellent that contains DEET
Drink only boiled or chlorinated water
bank.why: Also regular testing, no sharing of needles, safe blood transfusions, ART in pregnancy.

bank.q: Diseases of long duration and generally slow progression.
bank.why: Non-communicable, or chronic, diseases.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the 4 major categories of non-communicable diseases?
bank.why: The 4: cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, chronic respiratory diseases, cancer.

bank.q: The 4 major categories of non-communicable diseases are cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, cancer and...
bank.why: The 4 major NCDs are cardiovascular diseases, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases (like asthma and COPD) and diabetes. Tuberculosis, dengue and hepatitis are communicable.

bank.q: Another name for high blood pressure, which can increase the risk of heart disease, stroke and sometimes death.
bank.why: Hypertension = high blood pressure.

bank.q: The force that a person's blood exerts against the walls of their blood vessels.
bank.why: Blood pressure is the force that the blood exerts against the walls of the blood vessels, recorded as systolic over diastolic (e.g. 120/80).

bank.q: The pressure in your blood vessels when your heart contracts and pumps blood to the body (the top number).
bank.why: Systolic: top number, the heart pumps.

bank.q: The pressure in your blood vessels when your heart relaxes between beats (the bottom number).
bank.why: Diastolic: bottom number, the heart rests.

bank.q: In a blood pressure reading of 120/80, which number is the systolic pressure?
bank.why: The top number, 120, is systolic; 80 is diastolic.

bank.q: According to the slides, a blood pressure reading of ____ or lower is considered normal.
bank.why: 120/80 or lower is normal.

bank.q: According to the slides, a blood pressure reading of ____ or higher is considered high (hypertension).
bank.why: 140/90 or higher.

bank.q: According to the slides, a reading of 110/60 is considered...
bank.why: The slide calls 110/60 too low (hypotension).

bank.q: In the blood pressure categories table, "Systolic less than 120 and diastolic less than 80" is...
bank.why: Normal: systolic less than 120 and diastolic less than 80.

bank.q: In the blood pressure categories table, "Systolic 120–129 and diastolic less than 80" is...
bank.why: Elevated: systolic 120–129 and diastolic less than 80.

bank.q: In the blood pressure categories table, "Systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89" is...
bank.why: High blood pressure (hypertension) stage 1: systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89.

bank.q: In the blood pressure categories table, "Systolic 140 or higher or diastolic 90 or higher" is...
bank.why: High blood pressure (hypertension) stage 2: systolic 140 or higher or diastolic 90 or higher.

bank.q: In the blood pressure categories table, "Systolic higher than 180 and/or diastolic higher than 120" is...
bank.why: Hypertensive crisis: systolic higher than 180 and/or diastolic higher than 120. Consult your doctor immediately.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the ways to reduce the risk of hypertension in the slides?
bank.why: Reduce salt, exercise, healthy weight, fresh natural foods, don't smoke, follow medical advice.

bank.q: Which is among the symptoms of high blood pressure in the slides?
bank.a: Pounding in your chest, neck or ears
bank.why: Severe headache, vision problems, difficulty breathing, fatigue, chest pain, pounding in the chest/neck/ears, blood in the urine, irregular heartbeat.

bank.q: A general term for conditions affecting the heart or blood vessels.
bank.why: CVD is usually associated with fatty deposits in the arteries and a higher risk of blood clots.

bank.q: CVD is usually associated with a build-up of fatty deposits inside the arteries, called...
bank.why: Atherosclerosis, plus an increased risk of blood clots.

bank.q: The exact cause of CVD isn't clear, but things that increase your risk of getting it are called...
bank.why: From the Causes of CVD slide.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the CVD risk factors in the slides?
bank.why: High blood pressure, smoking, high cholesterol, diabetes, inactivity, being overweight or obese, family history, ethnic background, other risk factors.

bank.q: Occurs when the flow of blood to the heart is blocked, most often by a buildup of fat, cholesterol and other substances that form a plaque.
bank.why: Heart attack: blocked blood flow to the heart.

bank.q: The arteries that feed the heart are called the...
bank.why: Plaque forms in the coronary arteries.

bank.q: In a heart attack, what can happen when a plaque ruptures?
bank.a: It can form a clot that blocks blood flow
d: It dissolves and clears the artery
bank.why: Sometimes a plaque can rupture and form a clot.

bank.q: A sudden interruption in the blood supply of the brain.
bank.why: A stroke is a sudden interruption in the blood supply of the brain, either by a blockage (ischemic) or by bleeding (hemorrhagic).

bank.q: A stroke caused by an abrupt blockage of the arteries leading to the brain is called...
bank.why: Most strokes are ischemic.

bank.q: A stroke caused by bleeding into brain tissue when a blood vessel bursts is called...
bank.why: Hemorrhagic stroke: bleeding into brain tissue when a blood vessel bursts. Ischemic stroke is the blockage type.

bank.q: Most strokes are...
bank.a: Ischemic, caused by an abrupt blockage
d: Hemorrhagic, caused by a burst vessel
bank.why: Most strokes are ischemic: an abrupt blockage of the arteries leading to the brain. The rest are hemorrhagic (a vessel bursts).

bank.q: Which is among the 10 symptoms of stroke in the slides?
bank.why: Confusion, difficulty understanding, dizziness, loss of balance, numbness, severe headache, trouble speaking, trouble walking, vision changes, weakness.

bank.q: A disease in which your blood glucose, or blood sugar, levels are too high.
bank.why: Diabetes: blood glucose (blood sugar) levels are too high, because the body makes too little insulin or can't use it well.

bank.q: A hormone that helps glucose get into your cells to give them energy.
bank.why: Insulin is the hormone that helps glucose from food get into the cells to give them energy. In type 1 diabetes the body does not make it.

bank.q: What are the three main types of diabetes?
bank.why: The three main types are type 1 (little or no insulin, mostly children and teens), type 2 (body can't use its insulin well, mostly adults) and gestational (during pregnancy).

bank.q: "Occurs most often in children and adolescents; the body makes very little or no insulin, so daily insulin injections are needed." Which type of diabetes is this?
bank.why: Type 1 diabetes: occurs most often in children and adolescents; the body makes very little or no insulin, so daily insulin injections are needed.

bank.q: "More common in adults, about 90% of all cases; the body does not make good use of the insulin it produces." Which type of diabetes is this?
bank.why: Type 2 diabetes: more common in adults, about 90% of all cases; the body does not make good use of the insulin it produces.

bank.q: "High blood glucose during pregnancy, with complications for mother and child; usually disappears after pregnancy." Which type of diabetes is this?
bank.why: Gestational diabetes: high blood glucose during pregnancy, with complications for mother and child; usually disappears after pregnancy.

bank.q: Type 2 diabetes accounts for about what share of all diabetes cases?
bank.why: Type 2 diabetes is more common in adults and makes up around 90% of all diabetes cases.

bank.q: The cornerstone of type 2 diabetes treatment is...
bank.a: A healthy lifestyle: more physical activity and a healthy diet
d: Daily insulin injections from the day of diagnosis
Surgery on the pancreas as soon as possible
bank.why: Over time most will also need oral drugs and/or insulin.

bank.q: Women who had gestational diabetes, and their children, are at increased risk of developing...
bank.why: Gestational diabetes is high blood glucose during pregnancy; the mother and her child have a higher risk of type 2 diabetes later in life.

bank.q: A group of diseases involving abnormal cell growth with the potential to invade or spread to other parts of the body.
bank.why: Cancer contrasts with benign tumors, which do not spread.

bank.q: Tumors that do not spread to other parts of the body are called...
bank.why: Benign tumors do not spread. Cancer (malignant growth) can invade or spread to other parts of the body.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the classifications of cancer in the slides?
bank.why: Carcinomas, sarcomas, leukemia, lymphomas, adenomas.

bank.q: "Begins in the skin or the tissue that covers the surface of internal organs and glands; usually forms solid tumors." Which classification of cancer is this?
bank.why: Carcinoma: Begins in the skin or the tissue that covers the surface of internal organs and glands; usually forms solid tumors.

bank.q: "Begins in the tissues that support and connect the body, such as fat, muscles, nerves, tendons, cartilage or bone." Which classification of cancer is this?
bank.why: Sarcoma: Begins in the tissues that support and connect the body, such as fat, muscles, nerves, tendons, cartilage or bone.

bank.q: "A cancer of the blood that begins when healthy blood cells change and grow uncontrollably." Which classification of cancer is this?
bank.why: Leukemia: A cancer of the blood that begins when healthy blood cells change and grow uncontrollably.

bank.q: "A cancer that begins in the lymphatic system, the network of vessels and glands that help fight infection." Which classification of cancer is this?
bank.why: Lymphoma: A cancer that begins in the lymphatic system, the network of vessels and glands that help fight infection.

bank.q: "Arises in the thyroid, pituitary gland, adrenal gland and other glandular tissues." Which classification of cancer is this?
bank.why: Adenoma: Arises in the thyroid, pituitary gland, adrenal gland and other glandular tissues.

bank.q: Which type of cancer is the most common?
bank.why: Carcinomas are the most common type.

bank.q: Prostate cancer, breast cancer, lung cancer and colorectal cancer are examples of...
bank.why: Carcinomas begin in the skin or the tissue covering organs and glands, and are the most common cancer: prostate, breast, lung and colorectal cancer.

bank.q: How many main types of leukemia are there according to the slides?
bank.why: Acute lymphocytic, chronic lymphocytic, acute myeloid and chronic myeloid leukemia.

bank.q: What are the 2 main types of lymphoma?
bank.why: The 2 main types of lymphoma are Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin; the difference is the Reed-Sternberg cell, found in Hodgkin lymphoma.

bank.q: The main difference between Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the presence of which cells in Hodgkin lymphoma?
bank.why: Hodgkin: Reed-Sternberg cells, spreads in order from one lymph node group to another.

bank.q: Which lymphoma often spreads in an orderly way from one group of lymph nodes to another?
bank.why: Hodgkin lymphoma has Reed-Sternberg cells and often spreads in an orderly way from one group of lymph nodes to the next.

bank.q: Which lymphoma usually has no Reed-Sternberg cells, can spread in different patterns, and may develop from B cells or T cells?
bank.why: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma usually has no Reed-Sternberg cells, spreads in different patterns, and may come from B cells or T cells.

bank.q: Large, fast-growing, invasive, poorly differentiated tumors that metastasize are...
bank.why: Malignant tumors invade and destroy surrounding tissue, then metastasize.

bank.q: Small, slow-growing, non-invasive, well-differentiated tumors that stay localized are...
bank.why: Benign tumors stay where they are and can't invade or metastasize.

bank.q: According to the slides, one early cancer warning sign you shouldn't ignore is...
bank.why: "One symptom you shouldn't ignore: unexplained weight loss."

notes: Basics

Bill of Rights — Article III of the 1987 Constitution; 22 sections | Concept — declaration and enumeration of rights protected against the government or other people | Also — a charter of liberties and a limitation on the power of the State
Section 1

Due process — fair procedure: notice, a chance to defend yourself, fair treatment | Equal protection — everyone treated equally regardless of race, religion, gender, status, nationality, beliefs | Protects — life, liberty and property
Right to liberty (5 parts)

Right to exist — live, not deprived without lawful reason | Free from restraint or servitude — no slavery, forced labor, unjust imprisonment | Right to contract — leases, jobs, businesses | Choose one's employment — your own job or profession | Right to labor — work and earn a living; safe, fair conditions
Crimes against person

Homicide — killing without a qualifying circumstance | Murder — killing with treachery or evident premeditation | Parricide — killing family members | Infanticide — newborn less than 3 days old | Abortion | Giving assistance to suicide | Physical injuries — serious (disability), slight (bruises) | Rape
Crimes against liberty

Kidnapping — carrying away against their will | Illegal detention — keeping someone from leaving | Serious illegal detention — abducting and holding captive | Coercion — forcing through violence or threats | Grave threats — threatening a serious crime | Unlawful arrest — fake officer arrests | Human trafficking — fake job offer, exploitation | Arbitrary detention — by a public officer
Crimes against property

Robbery — with violence or force | Theft — without violence | Qualified theft — employee steals from employer | Estafa — swindling by deceit | Arson — setting fire | Malicious mischief — smashing windows | Carnapping — motor vehicles | Fencing — dealing in stolen goods | Trespass to property | Forgery — falsifying documents or signatures
Section 2: search and seizure

Covers — persons, houses, papers and effects | Warrant needs — probable cause determined personally by the judge, after examination under oath | Must describe — the place to be searched, persons or things to be seized | Person — citizens and aliens, accused or not | Houses — also garages, warehouses, shops, offices, safety deposit vaults | Papers and effects — includes sealed letters and packages | Consent — makes a search legal (James at the bus stop)
Warrants

Search warrant — written order signed by a judge, directed to a peace officer, to search for property and bring it to court | Warrant of arrest — written order by the judge to take a person into custody to answer for an offense
Section 3: privacy
Rule — communication and correspondence are inviolable | Exceptions — lawful court order; public safety or order as prescribed by law | Evidence obtained illegally — inadmissible for any purpose
Sections 4–11

4 — speech, expression, press, assembly, petition | 5 — religion; no religious test | 6 — abode (court order) and travel (national security, public safety, public health) | 7 — information on public concern | 8 — form unions, associations | 9 — just compensation | 10 — non-impairment of contracts | 11 — free access to courts despite poverty
Sections 12–17

12 — custodial investigation: silent, counsel (provided if poor), waiver only in writing with counsel; no torture or secret detention; forced confessions inadmissible | 13 — bail, except reclusion perpetua with strong evidence; surety or recognizance; still applies when habeas corpus is suspended | 14 — rights of the accused: presumed innocent, counsel, know the charges, speedy public trial, confront witnesses; trial in absentia after arraignment | 15 — habeas corpus; suspended only in invasion or rebellion | 16 — speedy disposition of cases | 17 — against self-incrimination; burden of proof on the government
Sections 18–22

18 — no detention for political beliefs; no involuntary servitude except as punishment after conviction | 19 — no excessive fines or cruel punishment; death penalty only if Congress provides for heinous crimes, else reclusion perpetua | 20 — no prison for debt or poll tax | 21 — double jeopardy | 22 — no ex post facto law (retroactive), no bill of attainder (guilty without trial)
Leadership
Leadership — the ability to influence and guide followers or members of an organization | Also — the ability to motivate people to accomplish goals
10 characteristics of a good leader

Vision — knows where to go, makes people believe | Wit — sound judgment even in crucial situations | Passion — intensely obsessed with their focus | Compassion — for supporters and followers | Charisma — captivating, charming, draws people | Communication skills — great orators and persuaders | Persistence — goals despite obstacles | Integrity — walk the talk, keep promises | Daring — bold, takes risks amid fear | Discipline — self-control and order
Traits of a leader: Maxwell (1999)
Six C's — character, charisma, commitment, communication, competence, courage
Transactional vs transformational

Transactional — corrective action, rewards only when expectations are met; tells each person what, when and how; power through rewards and coercion (patronage, colonization, vote-buying) | Transformational — starts from members' needs, rewards related to effort; trusts subordinates, gives space to grow; lives out values, approachable, accepts pressure to perform | Definition — broadens and elevates employees' interests, builds acceptance of the group's mission, looks beyond self-interest | Summary — a framework that brings people together around a common vision
13 behaviors of a transformational leader

1 — articulate, compelling vision of the future | 2 — stories and symbols | 3 — strong sense of purpose and collective mission | 4 — talks optimistically, confident goals will be met | 5 — does the right thing, not just things right | 6 — instills pride | 7 — talks about values and beliefs | 8 — moral and ethical consequences | 9 — seeks different perspectives | 10 — challenge old assumptions | 11 — teaching and coaching | 12 — each employee's needs, abilities, aspirations | 13 — compassionate, appreciative, celebrates achievements
4 components of transformational leadership

Individualized (idealized) influence — role model | Inspirational motivation — positive attitude that inspires | Intellectual stimulation — involve teams in decisions, creativity, innovation | Individualized consideration — relationships, individual support
Virtuous cycle of leadership control
1 — energetic, sympathetic, friendly, understanding → enthusiastic cooperation | 2 — confidence in the job → confidence of followers | 3 — be an example to followers
7 habits of highly effective people

Be proactive — take responsibility for your life | Begin with the end in mind — know where you want to go | Put first things first — self-management | Think win-win — cooperative, not competitive | Seek first to understand — listen | Synergize — better as a group | Sharpen the saw — keep updated, sense of humor
Teamwork, time, decisions

Teamwork — working collaboratively with a group to achieve a goal | Time management — arranging, organizing, scheduling, budgeting time for productivity | Decision-making — selecting the most logical choice from two or more options | Considerations — identify alternatives → evaluate options → select the best
8 kinds of involvement in decision-making

Consensus — compromise after all opinions are heard | Majority — voting | Minority — a few powerful personalities dominate | Silent consensus — agreement without discussion; unanimous; rarely for important issues | Clique — small group plans beforehand | Handclasp — one suggests, another commends | One-person decision — quick, but hard to get support later | Plop — deciding by not deciding
7 difficulties in decision-making

Fear of consequences — division, disagreement | Conflicting loyalties — member of different groups | Interpersonal conflicts — personal differences | Hidden agenda — secret motive | Blundering methods — rigid procedure, opinions over information | Inadequate leadership — restricts opinions | Clash of interest — opposing interests
Disease triangle

Model — interaction of host, agent and environment; predicts outcomes in plant and public health | Host — age, sex, race, genes, previous diseases, immune status, religion, customs, occupation, marital status, family | Environment — temperature, humidity, altitude, crowding, housing, water, milk, food, radiation, pollution, noise | Agent — biologic (bacteria, viruses), chemical (poison, alcohol, smoke), physical (trauma, radiation, fire), nutritional (lack, excess)
Communicable diseases

Definition — spread from person to person, "catching", caused by germs or pathogens | Pathogens — viruses, bacteria, parasitic worms, fungi | Food and water — cholera, typhoid, hepatitis (jaundice) | Air — influenza, tuberculosis | Mosquito — malaria | Bite wound with dust or rust — tetanus
Dengue fever

Cause — one of 4 virus serotypes, genus Flavivirus, family Flaviviridae | Symptoms — fever, rash, rapid pulse, dizziness, adynamia, insomnia, red eyes and throat, pain in the bones, anorexia, vomiting | Prevention — mosquitoes bite in the daytime; repellent (DEET, picaridin, IR3535); long sleeves, permethrin on clothes; screens, no standing water
Malaria

Cause — Plasmodium parasite (falciparum most serious; vivax, ovale, malariae) | Vector — female Anopheles mosquito | Symptoms — flu-like, diarrhea, vomiting, joint pains, fever; a week up to a year after infection | Treatment — depends on type, age, severity | Prevention — anti-malarial drugs, avoid bites
Cholera

Cause — Vibrio cholerae in food or water; incubation under 1 day to 5 days | Signs — diarrhea, vomiting, loss of skin elasticity, low blood pressure, increased thirst, rapid weight loss | Prevention — boiled or chlorinated water, handwashing, wash fruits and vegetables, cook properly, eat hot food; report diarrhea
Avian influenza and H1N1

Bird flu — influenza A viruses chiefly in birds | Bird flu signs — cough, high fever, fatigue, headache, nose bleed, runny nose, upset stomach, loss of appetite | Bird flu prevention — avoid poultry and droppings, cook poultry and eggs, wash hands, avoid wet and live poultry markets abroad, mask if unwell | H1N1 — swine flu; quadruple reassortant: 2 pig + 2 bird flu genes | H1N1 signs — systemic fever; psychological lethargy, lack of appetite; nasopharynx runny nose, sore throat; respiratory cough; gastric nausea, vomiting; intestinal diarrhea | H1N1 prevention — vaccine (only preventable respiratory virus), wash hands, sanitizer, don't touch face, eat right, exercise, stay home 24 h after fever
Typhoid fever

Cause — Salmonella typhi; S. paratyphi milder | Spread — human carrier deposits bacteria in food or water | Signs — white coating on the tongue, enlarged liver and spleen, rash, intestinal ulcers, high fever, delirium, abdominal pain, diarrhea or constipation | Prevention — hygiene, clean water, sewage disposal, fly control, wash food, cook well, no raw eggs, don't keep food warm or reheat
HIV/AIDS

HIV — attacks CD4 (T-helper) cells | AIDS — most advanced stage | Spread — unprotected sex, sharing needles, infected blood (rare now: screening), mother-to-child, needlestick (occupational) | Early stage — 2–4 weeks; flu-like | Clinical latency — no symptoms for years; 5–10 years untreated | AIDS stage — weight loss, night sweats, chronic diarrhea, TB, pneumonia, memory loss | Effects — immune failure, neurological, social and psychological (stigma), economic | Treatment — no cure; ART suppresses the virus | PrEP — before, for high risk | PEP — within 72 hours after exposure | Prevention — condoms, testing, no shared needles, safe transfusions, ART in pregnancy
Non-communicable diseases
Definition — long duration, slow progression (chronic) | 4 major — cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, chronic respiratory diseases, cancer
Blood pressure

Blood pressure — force of blood on vessel walls | Systolic — top number, heart pumps | Diastolic — bottom number, heart rests | Normal — 120/80 or lower | High — 140/90 or higher | Low (slides) — 110/60 hypotension | Table — normal <120 and <80; elevated 120–129 and <80; stage 1 130–139 or 80–89; stage 2 ≥140 or ≥90; crisis >180 and/or >120 | Reduce risk — less salt, exercise, healthy weight, fresh food, no smoking, medical advice
Heart, stroke, diabetes

CVD — heart or blood vessels; atherosclerosis, clots | CVD risk factors — high BP, smoking, high cholesterol, diabetes, inactivity, overweight, family history, ethnic background | Heart attack — blocked flow to the heart; plaque in coronary arteries; rupture → clot | Stroke — sudden interruption of blood to the brain; ischemic (blockage, most) or hemorrhagic (vessel bursts) | Diabetes — high blood glucose; insulin moves glucose into cells | Type 1 — children, little or no insulin, daily injections | Type 2 — adults, ~90%, poor use of insulin; healthy lifestyle | Gestational — in pregnancy; later type 2 risk
Cancer

Cancer — abnormal cell growth that can invade or spread; benign tumors don't spread | Carcinoma — skin or lining of organs and glands; most common (prostate, breast, lung, colorectal) | Sarcoma — supporting and connective tissue (fat, muscle, bone, cartilage) | Leukemia — blood; 4 types (ALL, CLL, AML, CML) | Lymphoma — lymphatic system; Hodgkin (Reed-Sternberg cells, orderly spread) vs non-Hodgkin | Adenoma — thyroid, pituitary, adrenal, glandular tissue | Benign — small, slow, localized | Malignant — large, fast, invasive, metastasize | Warning sign — unexplained weight loss
